actions.result: INR 5.4 (venous confirmation sample), prior stable INR 2.5-3.1 x 2 years

actions.name: Review CBC for bleeding workup
actions.result: Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL (baseline 13.0 g/dL 3 months ago), Hct 38%, platelets 230 x10^3/uL - no significant drop

actions.name: Review renal function (creatinine/eGFR)
actions.result: Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m2 - normal, no accumulation concern from renal impairment

actions.name: Review liver function tests
actions.result: AST 24 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL - all within normal limits

actions.name: Review current outpatient medication list in EHR
actions.result: Warfarin 5 mg daily, metoprolol tartrate 50 mg twice daily, acetaminophen PRN, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS twice daily x10 days (started 6 days ago, urgent care), turmeric-ginger supplement (self-added, not in EHR until today)

actions.name: Review urgent-care visit note for UTI
actions.result: Diagnosed uncomplicated cystitis, prescribed TMP-SMX DS BID x10 days; note states 'no other medications reported by patient'; no mention of warfarin or anticoagulation clinic

actions.name: Review INR trend over past 6 months
actions.result: INR stable 2.6-3.1 until this week; sharp rise to 5.4 coinciding with antibiotic start and dietary changes

actions.name: Perform bleeding risk screen (gums, skin, stool, neuro symptoms) via patient self-report and camera
actions.result: Patient shows gum oozing after brushing and a 6 cm bruise on left thigh on camera; denies black/tarry stools, denies headache, denies vision changes, denies blood in urine beyond prior UTI symptoms

actions.name: Perform structured medication reconciliation using OTC/herbal screening checklist
actions.result: Patient identifies turmeric-ginger joint supplement started 2 weeks ago, taken daily; no other new OTC products identified

actions.name: Review dietary/vitamin K intake pattern using structured nutrition screening tool
actions.result: Screening indicates reduced overall food intake and notably less leafy green vegetable consumption over the past 10 days compared to usual pattern

actions.name: Mechanical valve / stroke risk review
actions.result: Mechanical mitral valve, target INR range 2.5-3.5 confirmed from cardiology record; patient has no history of valve thrombosis or TIA

actions.name: Review anticoagulation clinic protocol for supratherapeutic INR with minor bleeding
actions.result: Protocol: for INR 5.0-9.0 with minor bleeding, hold warfarin, recheck INR in 24-48h, resume at reduced dose when therapeutic, address contributing cause. Protocol notes oral vitamin K 1-2.5 mg 'may be considered' if bleeding risk is elevated, but current CHEST (2022) guidance favors holding warfarin alone without routine vitamin K for INR 4.5-10 without major bleeding; given this patient's mechanical valve, empiric vitamin K carries overcorrection and valve thrombosis risk and should be reserved for INR >10 or major bleeding, with any use discussed with cardiology/prescriber first.

actions.name: Adherence assessment (pill count / dosing pattern)
actions.result: Patient reports taking warfarin 5 mg every evening without missed doses; home pill organizer confirms no missed doses in past 2 weeks

artifacts.title: Anticoagulation Clinic Collaborative Practice Protocol Excerpt
artifacts.author: Anticoagulation Clinic Pharmacy Service
artifacts.body: Supratherapeutic INR management (mechanical valve patients, no major bleeding): INR 5.0-9.0 with minor bleeding (e.g., gum bleeding, bruising) - hold warfarin 1-2 doses, recheck INR in 24-48 hours, resume warfarin at reduced dose once INR <3.5, identify and address precipitating cause (drug interaction, dietary change, adherence). Oral vitamin K 1-2.5 mg 'may be considered' if bleeding risk is felt to be elevated, but note that current CHEST (2022) guidance for INR 4.5-10 without major bleeding generally favors holding warfarin alone without routine vitamin K; in mechanical valve patients, unnecessary vitamin K risks overcorrection and valve thrombosis, so this should only be used after discussion with the covering cardiologist/prescriber. Notify prescribing cardiologist/surgeon for mechanical valve patients given thrombosis risk if dose held >48 hours without bridging discussion.

artifacts.title: Cardiology Note - Mechanical Mitral Valve, 1 Year Ago
artifacts.author: Cardiology
artifacts.body: Patient with mechanical mitral valve (St. Jude bileaflet), implanted 2 years ago. Anticoagulation with warfarin required lifelong, target INR 2.5-3.5 given mitral position and mechanical valve type. No bridging with heparin products indicated for routine supratherapeutic INR without major bleeding; manage per anticoagulation clinic protocol. Patient counseled extensively on vitamin K dietary consistency and drug interactions, including sulfonamide antibiotics and NSAIDs.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes the antibiotic doesn't count as a real medication change since it's temporary, and did not think it was relevant to disclose to the warfarin prescriber.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Urgent care note explicitly documents 'no other medications reported by patient' with no mention of warfarin or anticoagulation, despite patient being on warfarin for a mechanical valve.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may not recognize short-term or 'natural' therapies as medication changes worth disclosing; pharmacists must proactively screen for all new prescriptions, OTCs, and supplements at every encounter, especially around high-risk interacting drug classes like sulfonamides with warfarin.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she has not changed her warfarin dose on her own and takes exactly what is prescribed.
mismatches.recordEvidence: INR trend chart shows stable therapeutic INR values for 6 months with a sharp isolated spike to 5.4 only in the past week, consistent with an external precipitant (drug interaction/dietary change) rather than dosing error, supporting the patient's adherence claim rather than contradicting it.
mismatches.teachingPoint: When a mismatch is suspected, trend data can either confirm or refute patient self-report; here the trend supports adherence and redirects attention to the antibiotic interaction and dietary vitamin K reduction as the true cause, modeling that not all apparent discrepancies indicate nonadherence.

objectives.text: Elicit a best possible medication history including prescription, OTC, and herbal/supplement use, identifying the recently started antibiotic and turmeric-ginger supplement as contributors to supratherapeutic INR.
Recognize trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as a clinically significant CYP2C9 interaction with warfarin and correlate the interaction timeline with the INR trend.
Assess dietary vitamin K intake changes (fasting, reduced leafy greens) as a contributing factor to INR elevation.
Perform a structured bleeding risk assessment via camera and self-report, distinguishing minor bleeding (gum, bruise) from major/life-threatening bleeding warranting emergency referral.

Apply the anticoagulation clinic's collaborative practice protocol to recommend holding warfarin, considering oral vitamin K, and scheduling an INR recheck, while identifying when physician/cardiology notification is required for a mechanical valve patient.
Identify and resolve the mismatch between patient-reported adherence/communication and documentation in the urgent care note, using chart evidence appropriately rather than assuming nonadherence.

patient.name: Fatima Al-Sayed

Her affect is alert and articulate but visibly anxious, with hands occasionally gesturing to emphasize numbers she mentions.

persona.communicationStyle: Direct and organized, references specific dates and values, but downplays things she doesn't think are 'real' medication changes.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious about stroke risk, slightly embarrassed about not disclosing the supplement and antibiotic context, but cooperative once reassured.
persona.background: Has taught high school chemistry for over 20 years in Dearborn, Michigan. Lives with her husband; two adult children live out of state. Enjoys gardening and hosting family for Friday dinners. Became very engaged with her own health literacy after her valve surgery two years ago, keeping a detailed log of INR readings.

I know I'm supposed to tell you about new medicines, I just didn't think the antibiotic or the turmeric really counted.
If you hold my warfarin, how long until it's safe again? I need exact numbers.
I've been fasting this week, so I haven't eaten my usual greens - could that be part of it?
Please don't tell me I need to stop the warfarin completely, I'm worry about my valve.

Embarrassment about not telling the urgent care doctor about her warfarin

profile.summary: A 56-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on long-term warfarin presents to an anticoagulation clinic telehealth visit with a home INR of 5.4 confirmed by venous draw, minor mucocutaneous bleeding, and no major bleeding signs. The case teaches pharmacy learners to identify a classic multifactorial cause (undisclosed TMP-SMX antibiotic interaction plus reduced dietary vitamin K intake and an unreported herbal supplement), perform a remote bleeding assessment, and apply a collaborative practice protocol for supratherapeutic INR management with appropriate escalation to the cardiology/prescribing team.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Dearborn, Michigan, seated at her kitchen table

answerKey.primaryProblem: Supratherapeutic INR (5.4) in a mechanical mitral valve patient on chronic warfarin, with minor bleeding, due to a multifactorial drug-drug and drug-diet interaction (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus reduced vitamin K intake, compounded by an unreported turmeric-ginger supplement).
differential: Drug-drug interaction (TMP-SMX potentiating warfarin via CYP2C9 inhibition) - most likely primary cause given temporal correlation
Dietary vitamin K reduction from fasting and decreased leafy green intake - contributing factor
Herbal supplement (turmeric-ginger) with possible additive antiplatelet/anticoagulant effect - contributing factor
Warfarin nonadherence or dosing error - ruled out by patient report and pill organizer confirmation; INR trend supports no dosing change
Underlying hepatic dysfunction or renal impairment affecting warfarin metabolism/clearance - ruled out by normal LFTs and renal function
New major bleeding source (GI, intracranial) - ruled out by negative bleeding review of systems (no melena, no neuro symptoms, stable hemoglobin)
keyFindings: Home and lab-confirmed INR 5.4 (target 2.5-3.5) with minor bleeding (gum bleeding, large thigh bruise)
No signs of major/life-threatening bleeding: no melena, no neuro symptoms, stable hemoglobin and platelets
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole started 6 days ago for UTI without disclosure to warfarin prescriber - known significant CYP2C9 interaction
Reduced vitamin K intake from fasting and decreased leafy green vegetables over past 10 days
Previously undisclosed turmeric-ginger supplement started 2 weeks ago
INR trend stable 2.6-3.1 for 6 months, abrupt isolated rise this week - supports acute precipitant rather than chronic nonadherence
Mechanical mitral valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; brief dose holds are standard but prolonged interruption raises thrombosis risk
plan: Hold warfarin per collaborative practice protocol given INR 5.0-9.0 with minor bleeding; do not administer bridging anticoagulation for routine supratherapeutic INR without major bleeding

Do not routinely give oral vitamin K for this INR/bleeding level per current CHEST (ACCP) antithrombotic guidance; reserve vitamin K for INR >10 or major bleeding, and if considered despite minor bleeding, discuss with cardiology first given overcorrection/valve thrombosis risk in a mechanical valve patient
Recommend INR recheck in 24-48 hours either via clinic lab or home monitor with lab confirmation
Advise patient to discontinue turmeric-ginger supplement until cleared by anticoagulation team given its potential additive bleeding risk
Counsel patient to maintain consistent (not necessarily increased) vitamin K intake going forward rather than drastic changes

Communicate with urgent care/UTI prescriber or patient's PCP regarding the warfarin-TMP/SMX interaction; consider whether antibiotic course needs adjustment in consultation with prescriber - this decision is outside pharmacist's unilateral authority and requires prescriber communication
Notify cardiology per protocol given mechanical valve status if warfarin hold is anticipated to exceed 48 hours without a recheck plan
Reinforce patient education: all new prescriptions, OTC medications, and supplements must be disclosed to the anticoagulation clinic going forward, including when a medication seems 'temporary'
Monitor for signs of major bleeding (melena, hematemesis, neuro symptoms) and provide clear emergency instructions to seek immediate in-person care if these occur
Plan to resume warfarin at reduced or prior dose only once INR trends below 3.5, per protocol, with close follow-up INR monitoring
redFlags: Any report of black/tarry stools, hematemesis, hemoptysis, severe headache, neurological deficits, or heavy uncontrolled bleeding would require immediate referral to emergency care rather than routine protocol management

INR greater than 9 or any major bleeding would require different protocol pathway (e.g., higher-dose vitamin K, possible emergency department evaluation) rather than outpatient telehealth management alone
Prolonged warfarin interruption without a recheck/resumption plan carries valve thrombosis risk and requires explicit cardiology coordination
Routine administration of vitamin K for minor bleeding at INR 5.0-9.0 (rather than reserving it for INR >10 or major bleeding) risks overcorrection and valve thrombosis in a mechanical valve patient
educationPoints: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a well-documented potent inhibitor of CYP2C9 and significantly potentiates warfarin's anticoagulant effect; patients and non-anticoagulation prescribers often underappreciate this interaction
Patients may not recognize short-course antibiotics or 'natural' supplements as medication changes relevant to disclose - proactive, structured screening at every encounter is essential
Dietary vitamin K consistency, not elimination, is the appropriate counseling message; sudden reductions (e.g., during fasting periods) can destabilize INR as much as sudden increases
Many herbal supplements (turmeric, ginger, fish oil, vitamin E) carry additive bleeding or anticoagulant-potentiating risk and should be systematically screened for in anticoagulation management

Collaborative practice protocols give pharmacists authority to manage routine supratherapeutic INR, but major bleeding, valve thrombosis concerns, or care coordination with other prescribers (e.g., urgent care) require timely communication and may exceed pharmacist unilateral scope

Current CHEST (2022) guidance for INR 4.5-10 without major bleeding generally favors holding warfarin alone without routine vitamin K; routine vitamin K use in this range, especially in a mechanical valve patient, risks overcorrection and valve thrombosis and should not be presented as a default protocol step without this caveat
Clear, numeric, stepwise communication (dose, recheck timing, when to resume) helps address anxious patients' need for concrete guidance while reinforcing safety
